paras: The killing of Jim Vance was the shooting of Jim (James) Vance, an older man linked to the Hatfield faction, by an armed party of Kentuckians in Logan County, West Virginia, in early January 1888. The party had come from Pike County, Kentucky, to hunt the Hatfields after a New Year's night raid on the home of Randolph McCoy, and later seized nine West Virginia men. Kentucky reports described a posse fighting the 'Hatfield gang', while West Virginia sources called the killing the murder of 'old man Vance' by men with no legal authority.

Papers traced the feud to the 1882 election-day killing of Ellison Hatfield in Pike County and the killing of several McCoys in reprisal, for which Hatfield men were indicted in Kentucky. In September 1887 Governor Buckner of Kentucky offered a reward for the Hatfields, but Governor Wilson of West Virginia did not honor the requisition. On New Year's night a band burned Randolph McCoy's house on Peter Creek, killing a son and a daughter and beating his wife; Kentucky papers charged the raid to the Hatfields, who denied any part in it.

According to a Frankfort dispatch, Pikeville people armed themselves and 'about thirty men formed a party to avenge the outrage' in Logan County. The Hartford Herald, a Kentucky paper, said the band was led by Frank Phillips, a former Pike County deputy sheriff whom Buckner had named to receive prisoners, and crossed into West Virginia on January 8. Another Kentucky dispatch said the 'thirty avengers' had no connection with the authorities.

The Herald said the band was fired on by 'old Jim Vance' and Cap Hatfield and that Vance was killed in the fight that followed. Valentine Hatfield, later a prisoner of the Kentuckians, said the Pike County men found Vance and Cap Hatfield on a bridge near Thacker's creek, shot Vance to death and wounded Cap Hatfield. Governor Wilson's emissary reported that the party 'fired on and killed old man Vance without as much as calling him to surrender.'
Early reports gave more dead: the Frankfort dispatch named John Hatfield, a Catlettsburg wire said three of the Hatfield party died in a fight in the woods, and another added a Jeff Nicolls.

Logan County issued warrants for six of the Kentucky party for Vance's murder, and on about January 21 a constable's guard serving them was fired on near Grapevine and William Dempsey was killed. A Kentucky wire told that fight as a Hatfield ambush and said 'the man that killed Jim Vance on the first raid' shot the dying Dempsey in the head. No report of an inquest or trial for Vance's death appears in the coverage.

Wilson's emissary, Col. W. L. Mahon, reported on January 31 that the Pike County men had 'kidnaped' nine West Virginians, including Thomas Chambers and Valentine Hatfield, and on February 1 Wilson requisitioned eight of them. By February 17 the nine were in the Louisville jail awaiting a federal habeas corpus hearing, while Pike County attorney J. Lee Ferguson argued that the Kentuckians had been justified in acting themselves.

Most first dispatches came from Catlettsburg, Kentucky, and spoke of a 'war of extermination' by a 'McCoy posse' against the 'Hatfield gang'; papers from Wheeling to Red Cloud, Nebraska, reprinted them. West Virginia papers pushed back: the Wheeling Register headlined the Logan letter 'The McCoys Again the Aggressors', and the Wheeling Intelligencer complained of Kentucky reports' 'decided coloring in favor of the McCoy faction.' The Intelligencer also reprinted a Pittsburgh Times editorial, 'West Virginia Barbarians,' which suggested that a 'Judge Lynch's Court' might redeem the state.
Valentine Hatfield's account ran in Memphis and Wheeling on February 18, while the Hartford Herald called Vance one of the worst of the gang and Wilson either timid or corrupt.

Only Vance is named as killed in every detailed account; a second death, John Hatfield, rests on the Frankfort dispatch alone. In December 1888 the Big Sandy News of Louisa, Kentucky, reported that Johnson Hatfield had just died of illness nearby under the name Vance. That Vance fired first is a Kentucky claim; that he was shot without a call to surrender comes from the Hatfield side and Wilson's emissary.

reader.title: Killing of Jim Vance
bases: An armed party of Pike County, Kentucky, men hunting the Hatfield faction, called a 'posse' in Kentucky wires and a band without legal authority in West Virginia accounts, shot Jim Vance in Logan County (A4, A14, A19).

A party of twenty to thirty Kentuckians, formed 'to avenge the outrage' of the New Year's raid and described even by a Kentucky dispatch as acting with 'no connection with the authorities', killed Vance in West Virginia without warrants (A11, A12, A14); it is probable rather than certain because a Kentucky account says Vance fired first and died in an exchange of fire (A19).

Vance's killing by the Kentucky party is reported independently by Kentucky wires and papers, a Logan County letter, the West Virginia governor's emissary, and Valentine Hatfield (A6, A9, A12, A14, A17, A19), though they disagree on how it happened and on other dead.

accounts.label: Catlettsburg wire (Kentucky)
accounts.gist: A McCoy posse went into West Virginia 'for the purpose of annihilating the gang', was attacked in the woods, and killed three of the Hatfield party without loss; a later wire added Jeff Nicolls as dead.

accounts.label: Frankfort/Louisville dispatch
accounts.gist: About thirty Pikeville men formed a party to avenge the New Year's raid, went into Logan County, and killed Jim Vance and John Hatfield.

accounts.label: Hartford Herald (Kentucky)
accounts.gist: Frank Phillips's armed band crossed on Jan. 8 and was fired on by old Jim Vance and Cap Hatfield; Vance was killed in the fight that followed.

accounts.label: Valentine Hatfield (captive)
accounts.gist: A company of Pike County men formed to follow and kill the Hatfields found Vance and Cap Hatfield on a bridge near Thacker's creek, shot Vance to death and wounded Cap Hatfield.

accounts.label: Gov. Wilson's emissary (Mahon)
accounts.gist: The Phillips party had no requisition and fired on and killed old man Vance without calling on him to surrender.

accounts.label: Logan constable's guard (W. P. Floyd)
accounts.gist: The Kentucky gang murdered James Vance on West Virginia soil, and Logan warrants were issued for six of them.

framing.detail: Catlettsburg wires, widely reprinted, spoke of a 'war of extermination', a 'McCoy posse' and the 'Hatfield gang', and blamed the Hatfields for the raids.
The Wheeling Register ran the Logan letter under 'The McCoys Again the Aggressors' and called Vance's death a murder by Kentucky men who had 'invaded West Virginia soil'.

The Wheeling Intelligencer accused Kentucky correspondents of 'a decided coloring in favor of the McCoy faction' while also printing a Kentucky account sympathetic to the McCoys and a Pittsburgh editorial that mused on 'Judge Lynch's Court'.
The Hartford Herald (Kentucky) presented Vance as one of the worst of the gang who fired first, and called Gov. Wilson timid or corrupt.
